sections.text:
Solomon, peace be upon him, is the son of the Prophet David. He inherited prophecy and kingship from his father, but God endowed him with a great kingdom that he did not give to anyone before him and will not give to anyone after him.

Solomon prayed to his Lord, saying: “My Lord, forgive me and grant me a kingdom that no one after me should have. You are the Giver.”

God answered his prayer and made soldiers available to him that were not made available to any ordinary human being. The jinn, humans, birds, and winds were subjected to him!
The wind carried him and his army and his convoy, covering a month's journey in the morning, and another month's journey in the evening.

The jinn and divers would build towering palaces, statues, and niches for him, and extract pearls from the bottom of the oceans, and whoever among them rebelled would handcuff him.

God also taught him “bird logic,” that is, the language of birds and animals, so he would talk to them and understand them.

One day, while he was walking with his great army of jinn, humans, and birds, they passed a valley full of ants.

Solomon heard a wise ant warning her companions, saying: “O ants, enter your dwellings, lest Solomon and his soldiers destroy you while they are not aware.”

Solomon smiled and laughed at what the ant said, thanked God for this blessing, and ordered his army to change its course so as not to run over the weak ants.

In another situation, Suleiman inspected the bird and did not find the “hoopoe.” He became angry because of its absence without permission, and threatened it with punishment if he did not come up with a strong excuse.

The hoopoe came bearing great news. He found a kingdom in the land of Yemen called “Sheba”, ruled by a powerful queen (Bilqis), but they worshiped the sun instead of God!
Suleiman sent a message with the hoopoe to Bilqis inviting her to convert to Islam: “He is from Suleiman, and it is in the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful * that you do not rise above me and come to me in submission.”

Bilqis tried to appease Suleiman by sending valuable gifts of gold and jewelry to avoid war, but Suleiman strongly rejected her and stressed that he only wanted them to convert to Islam.

Belqis decided to go herself to meet Suleiman in Jerusalem.

To impress her and demonstrate God's power, Solomon asked his soldiers to bring Bilqis's huge throne from Yemen before her arrival!
A demon from the jinn volunteered to bring it before Solomon rose from his council, but a righteous man who had knowledge of the Book said: “I will bring it to you before your heart turns back to you” (before you even blink).

Indeed, he brought the throne in the twinkling of an eye, and Solomon bowed down to God in thanks.

When Bilqis arrived and saw her throne, she was impressed by Suleiman's intelligence and strength.

Then I entered his palace, and Solomon had ordered the jinn to build a transparent glass courtyard over a pool of water.

When Bilqis saw it, she thought it was real water, so she lifted her dress so that it would not get wet. Suleiman told her that it was a edifice made of smooth glass bottles.

Bilqis realized the weakness of her power before the king of Solomon, who was supported by God, so she submitted to God, Lord of the worlds, and said: “My Lord, I have wronged myself, and I submitted with Solomon to God, Lord of the worlds.”

Despite all this great kingship, Solomon was not arrogant, but was always thankful to God.

When his death came, God wanted to show the people and the jinn that the jinn do not know the unseen.

Solomon, peace be upon him, died leaning on his staff, standing and watching the jinn as they worked hard to build the Holy House.

He remained dead in that state for a long time (it was said that a year), and the jinn acted in fear of him, thinking that he was alive and watching them!
Until God sent the “earth” insect, which ate his stick from below, so his balance was lost and he fell to the ground dead.

Only then did the jinn realize that he had died, and people learned that if the jinn had known the unseen, they would not have remained in humiliating torment for all this time.

The lesson of Solomon’s story is that kingship, wealth, and power are blessings from God that must be harnessed to spread goodness, justice, and monotheism, and not for arrogance and tyranny.
